John Lightfoot
jon līt'-foot
n. (John Lightfoot, 1602–1675, Westminster divine, Master of Catharine Hall, rabbinic scholar)
Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Lightfoot, a byname for a swift runner.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

John Lightfoot was the greatest English rabbinic scholar of the seventeenth century and probably of any century before the nineteenth. Rector of Ashley and then of Great Munden, Master of Catharine Hall, Cambridge, and vice-chancellor of the university, he sat in the Westminster Assembly, where he kept the fullest surviving journal of its debates and argued the Erastian side on church government — the one point on which his brethren thought him wrong. His great work is the Horae Hebraicae et Talmudicae, a commentary on the Gospels, Acts, Romans and 1 Corinthians which illuminates the New Testament from the Mishnah, the Talmuds and the Midrashim, showing what a phrase of our Lord's meant to the men who first heard it. He laboured through the rabbinic literature at a time when almost no Christian did, and his notes are still cited. He studied the Jewish sources in order to read the Gospels better, which is the right order. “Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me” (Joh 5:39).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines the Talmud as the book which contains the Jewish traditions, and to expound as to explain or lay open the meaning.

expand to see more

TAL'MUD, n. The book which contains the Jewish traditions, the rabbinical constitutions and explications of the law.

EXPOUND', v.t. To explain; to lay open the meaning; to interpret.

RAB'BINICAL, a. Pertaining to the rabbins, or to their opinions, learning and language.

Key Scripture

Joh 5:39 — "Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me."

Luk 24:27 — "And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself."

2Ti 2:15 — "Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth."

Modern Corruption

The Assembly's rabbinic scholar, author of the Horae Hebraicae.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Lightfoot's method has however been turned on its head by a later scholarship which uses the Jewish background to relativise the text — treating the Gospels as one more first-century document to be explained by its environment. He used the background to make the text clearer about its own claims, which is the difference between illumination and dissolution.

The principle to recover is that all the searching of Scripture terminates in a person: the writings “are they which testify of me” (Joh 5:39), and our Lord himself, “beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luk 24:27). It is the glory of God to conceal a thing and the honour of the searcher to find it out (Pro 25:2).

Usage

"“they are they which testify of me” (Joh 5:39) — the aim of the Horae Hebraicae."

"“he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luk 24:27) — his controlling text."

"“the honour of kings is to search out a matter” (Pro 25:2) — forty years in the Talmuds."
